Chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) supports substantial commercial fisheries throughout its wide distribution in subtropical and temperate waters, and its life history traits have been examined across multiple ocean basins. Field studies consistently report that adult individuals attain a maximum total length of 64 cm [Li = 64 cm], representing the upper bound of somatic growth in this species. The egg diameter of this species, averaging approximately 1.05 mm, gives rise to a calculated wet weight at birth of 0.0006 grams [Wwb = 0.0006 grams], a minuscule starting mass that reflects the pelagic spawning strategy common among scombrids. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae rely entirely on endogenous reserves during the first days after hatching, and laboratory rearing trials indicate that the prolarvae emerge from the chorion after approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This brief embryonic period is characteristic of small pelagic eggs incubated under warm conditions and stands in contrast to the longer incubation times observed in larger demersal spawners within the same family.

Reproductive parameters in Chub mackerel have been quantified from histological examination of ovaries collected during spawning seasons across multiple years. Females release a substantial number of eggs across repeated spawning events, and the maximum annual reproductive output has been estimated at 1,860,000 eggs per year [Ri = 1,860,000 eggs per year] under optimal thermal conditions (20.7 °C [T = 20.7 °C]). This corresponds to multiple spawning events per year [F_R_i = multiple spawning events per year] when averaged over the year, though actual spawning is intermittent rather than continuous. The onset of gonadal maturation begins once individuals surpass a certain body size threshold; puberty is attained at a total length of 26.1 cm [Lp = 26.1 cm], a metric derived from extensive length-at-maturity ogives constructed from field-caught specimens. Fish below this length are nearly always immature, whereas a rapid transition to reproductive activity occurs once this size is reached during the second year of life.

Body mass increases dramatically from the larval stage through adulthood, and several key mass benchmarks have been established from length-weight regressions and direct field measurements. The wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 197 grams [Wwp = 197 grams], calculated from the allometric relationship between total length and body mass in wild-caught individuals. This value represents the mass at which gonadal recrudescence is first detectable and marks the transition from somatic investment toward the onset of reproductive allocation. At the opposite end of the growth trajectory, the ultimate wet weight for this species reaches approximately 2900 grams [Wwi = approximately 2900 grams] among the largest adults sampled in commercial catches. This asymptotic mass corresponds closely to the theoretical maximum body size derived from the von Bertalanffy growth equation fitted to length-at-age data from otolith readings spanning the entire geographic range of Scomber japonicus in the Pacific Ocean.

Longevity estimates for Chub mackerel are derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith age validation using annual increment counts. The maximum recorded lifespan in the wild reaches approximately 6,570 days [am = approximately 6,570 days] for individuals maintained at a water temperature of 20.7 °C [T = 20.7 °C], which corresponds to roughly 18 years. This extended lifespan is somewhat longer than that reported for some other small scombrids and reflects the species' position as a medium-bodied pelagic predator with relatively slow natural mortality rates once adulthood is achieved. Mortality schedules indicate that the highest attrition occurs during the early larval and juvenile stages, when predation pressure and starvation risk are elevated. The combination of high fecundity, a moderate age at first reproduction, and a protracted adult lifespan positions Scomber japonicus as an iteroparous strategist capable of multiple spawning seasons across its life cycle, a pattern that buffers population fluctuations against interannual variability in oceanographic conditions.

Feeding ecology and migratory behavior further shape the life history expression observed in Chub mackerel populations. This species undertakes extensive seasonal migrations between spawning grounds and feeding areas, tracking zooplankton biomass and forage fish concentrations across continental shelf regions. The energetic demands of these migrations are supported by a high metabolic rate typical of actively swimming scombrids, and individuals must accumulate sufficient lipid reserves during summer foraging bouts to sustain both overwintering survival and the subsequent reproductive season. Comparative studies with congeneric species such as Scomber colias and Scomber scombrus reveal that Scomber japonicus occupies an intermediate position in terms of both growth rate and maximum body size within the genus. Morphometric analyses confirm that the total length at puberty of approximately 26.1 cm [Lp = approximately 26.1 cm] corresponds closely to the inflection point of the length-weight relationship, after which mass gain per unit length increases substantially as energy is diverted toward gonadal development rather than continued somatic expansion. This life history configuration, combining rapid juvenile growth with delayed maturity until a relatively large body size, is consistent with the moderate predation risk and seasonal resource pulses characteristic of subtropical pelagic ecosystems.
